title: The Laplace transform
objectives: Compute Laplace transforms from the definition and a table.

screens.title: Paying for ever
screens.prose: A contract pays £1 a year, continuously, for ever. Money due at time $t$ is worth $e^{-st}$ today at rate $s$. The present value is the whole area under that curve. Slide the rate and watch the area.
screens.question: What is the contract worth at 4%?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the rate to 4% and read the area.

byKey.percent: You divided by 4, not by 0.04. Rates enter as decimals.

explain.text: The area is $\int_0^\infty e^{-0.04t}\,dt = 1/0.04 = 25$. A higher rate shrinks the area, as the slider showed.

screens.title: A name for the area
screens.prose:
Weight any cash flow $f(t)$ by $e^{-st}$ and add it up for ever:

$$F(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t)\,dt.$$

This is the **Laplace transform** of $f$, written $\mathcal{L}\{f\}$. Your £25 was $F(0.04)$ for $f(t) = 1$.
screens.question: Write $\mathcal{L}\{1\}$ as a function of $s$.

hints.text: What area did 4% give, and how does 25 depend on 0.04?
Let $b \to \infty$: the area is $1/s$ for every $s > 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $e^{-st}$ from 0 to infinity.

byKey.rate: That is the rate itself. The area under $e^{-st}$ is its reciprocal, $1/s$.

explain.text: $\int_0^\infty e^{-st}\,dt = 1/s$, so a perpetuity at rate $s$ is worth $1/s$. Every present value at a continuous rate is a Laplace transform.

screens.title: A growing cash flow
screens.prose: Let the cash flow grow: $f(t) = e^{at}$. Then $e^{-st}e^{at} = e^{-(s - a)t}$, the same curve with rate $s - a$. The rate here is $s = 6\%$. Slide the growth $a$ up past 6%.
screens.question: What is $\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\}$?

options.why: You added the rates. The exponents combine as $-(s - a)t$, so $a$ is subtracted.
You kept the formula past $s = a$. There the curve never falls, as the slider showed.
You moved $e^{a}$ out of the integral. The factor is $e^{at}$, which depends on $t$.

hints.text: That is the first screen's curve, with rate $s - a$ in place of $s$.
So the area is $1/(s - a)$, but only while $s - a > 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Combine the exponents first.

byKey.c: At $a \ge s$ the area kept growing. The formula needs $s > a$.

explain.text: The integrand is $e^{-(s - a)t}$, so the area is $1/(s - a)$ while $s > a$. At $s \le a$ the curve never falls and the area grows without bound.

screens.title: By parts: $f(t) = t$
screens.prose: For $f(t) = t$, integrate by parts with $u = t$ and $dv = e^{-st}\,dt$ (integrals lesson 10). The boundary term is 0 at both ends. What is left is $\tfrac{1}{s}\int_0^\infty e^{-st}\,dt$.
screens.question: What is $\mathcal{L}\{t\}$ at $s = 2$?

hints.text: Parts leaves $\tfrac1s$ times an integral you know.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Finish the parts step, then set $s = 2$.

byKey.no-square: That is $1/s$. Parts leaves $\tfrac1s\int_0^\infty e^{-st}\,dt$, which brings a second factor of $1/s$.
byKey.square: You found $s^2$. The transform is its reciprocal, $1/s^2$.

explain.text: $\int_0^\infty te^{-st}\,dt = \tfrac1s \cdot \tfrac1s = 1/s^2$, which is 0.25 at $s = 2$. The shaded area on the canvas is the same 0.25.

screens.title: Powers, sines and cosines
screens.prose: Two rounds of parts give $\mathcal{L}\{t^2\} = 2/s^3$. Sines and cosines also take two rounds. The canvas shades $e^{-t}\sin 3t$, so its signed area is $\mathcal{L}\{\sin 3t\}(1)$. Fill each value at $s = 1$.
screens.question: Fill the column $F(1)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Substitute $s = 1$ in each formula.

byKey.r1c2: Check the sine row. If you put $s$ on top, that is the cosine's transform; the sine has $b = 3$ on top.
byKey.r2c2: Check the cosine row. If you put $b$ on top, that is the sine's transform; the cosine has $s$ on top.

screens.title: A growing dividend
screens.prose: A share pays £5 a year, growing at 2%. Its value is $\mathcal{L}\{5e^{0.02t}\}(r) = \dfrac{5}{r - 0.02}$, which is £125 at $r = 6\%$: the Gordon growth model. Slide $r$ down to 1%.
screens.question: What is the share worth at $r = 1\%$?

options.why: You trusted the formula where the integral does not exist. With $r \le g$ the dividends never shrink.
You dropped the sign of $r - g$. Either way, the formula does not apply when $r \le g$.

options.text: No finite value: the integral diverges

options.why: You multiplied the transforms of 5 and $e^{0.02t}$. The transform of a product is not the product of transforms.

hints.text: Watch the caption as $r$ falls below 2%.
That grows for ever, so no finite area exists.

feedback.correct: At 1% the area has no limit, so the formula gives nonsense.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether the integral exists at 1%.

byKey.a: That is the trap: $1/(s - a)$ holds only for $s > a$. Here $s = 0.01 < 0.02$.
byKey.d: A product of cash flows has no product rule. Transform $5e^{0.02t}$ as one function.

explain.text: At 1% the dividends grow faster than they are discounted, and the caption's area kept growing. $\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\}$ exists only for $s > a$. A negative price is the formula used outside that range.

screens.title: No transform at all
screens.prose: Some functions grow too fast for any rate. The canvas draws $e^{t^2 - st}$. Slide $s$ as high as it goes and watch the far end of the curve.

state.caption: The curve is lowest at $t = s/2$, then climbs for ever.

screens.question: Which cash flow has no Laplace transform at any $s$?

options.why: That grows fast, but any $s > 5$ beats it: its transform is $1/(s - 5)$.
Any power loses to $e^{-st}$ when $s > 0$. Its transform is $10!/s^{11}$.
That stays between $-1$ and 1, so $e^{-st}$ makes it integrable for every $s > 0$.

hints.text: Compare the exponents $t^2$ and $st$ for large $t$.
$t^2 - st = t(t - s)$, positive once $t > s$.
So $e^{t^2 - st}$ grows for every $s$: $e^{t^2}$ has no transform.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the function no exponential can discount.

explain.text: $t^2 - st$ is positive once $t > s$, whatever $s$ is. So $e^{t^2 - st}$ grows without bound and no rate gives a finite area. Any piecewise continuous function growing no faster than some $e^{at}$ has a transform.

screens.title: The derivative rule
screens.prose: Take the transform of $f'$ and integrate by parts with $u = e^{-st}$ and $dv = f'(t)\,dt$. One line below is wrong; leave it out.
screens.question: Put the argument in order.

lines.why: A bracket is the upper value minus the lower value: $0 - f(0)$.

hints.text: Parts gives a bracket and an integral with $s$ in front.
The bracket is $0 - f(0)$, so $\mathcal{L}\{f'\} = sF(s) - f(0)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow parts line by line.

byKey.d1: The lower limit is subtracted: $[g]_0^\infty = g(\infty) - g(0)$.
byKey.left-out: Each correct line is needed; only the one with $+f(0)$ goes.

explain.text: Parts moves the derivative from $f$ onto $e^{-st}$, which brings out $s$. The boundary term at 0 leaves $-f(0)$. Applied twice, $\mathcal{L}\{f''\} = s^2F - sf(0) - f'(0)$, the rule lesson 15 runs on.

screens.title: Reading the table
screens.prose: Transforms add: $\mathcal{L}\{af + bg\} = aF + bG$. The **shift rule** handles an exponential factor: $$\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}f(t)\} = F(s - a).$$ So read $F$ from the table, then replace $s$ by $s - a$.
screens.question: What is $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-t}\cos 2t\}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shift the cosine's transform by $a = -1$.

byKey.sign: You shifted the wrong way. With $a = -1$, $s - a$ is $s + 1$.

explain.text: The cosine row gives $s/(s^2 + 4)$; the factor $e^{-t}$ shifts $s$ to $s + 1$. The result is $\dfrac{s + 1}{(s + 1)^2 + 4}$.

screens.title: Transforms in NumPy
screens.prose: A computer cuts the integral at $T = 50$ and uses the trapezium rule on $n$ strips. Write the sum out rather than calling a library routine. Then guard the growing perpetuity: no value exists when $r \le g$.

params.title: numpy
lines: ValueError: no value when r <= g

    ...

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests. Transforms are compared within absolute 1e-6 (1e-5 for $t^2$). Prices use `math.isclose` (relative 1e-9). The two divergent cases must raise `ValueError`. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: Build the grid with `np.linspace(0, T, n + 1)` and evaluate $e^{-st}f(t)$ on it.
The trapezium sum is $h$ times all the values, less half of the two end values.
`pv_growing` raises `ValueError` when `r <= g`, else returns `c / (r - g)`.

feedback.correct: Both pass: the trapezium values sit within $10^{-7}$ of 0.5, 0.25 and 0.3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the failing row: a transform off by a factor, or a missing `ValueError`.

explain.text: The trapezium rule on 200,000 strips is accurate to about $10^{-8}$ here; the cut at $T = 50$ costs below $10^{-18}$. The guard turns the trap into an error a pricer cannot ignore.

screens.title: A claim paid at default
screens.prose: A contract pays £100 when its issuer defaults. Default comes at hazard rate 2% a year, so its time has density $0.02e^{-0.02t}$. Discount at 4%. The value is $100\,\mathcal{L}\{0.02e^{-0.02t}\}(0.04)$. The moment generating function of `limits-thm` lesson 19 is this transform, read at $-s$.
screens.question: What is the claim worth?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Transform the density, then multiply by £100.

byKey.no-shift: You used $0.02/0.04$, as if default never thinned the payments. The density's own $e^{-0.02t}$ adds to the rate.
byKey.undiscounted: That is the payment with no discounting. A payment far in the future is worth less today.

explain.text: $\mathcal{L}\{0.02e^{-0.02t}\}(0.04) = 0.02/(0.04 + 0.02) = 1/3$. So the claim is worth £33.33, the area on the canvas. Discounting and default add their rates.

ideas: A present value at continuous rate $s$ is a Laplace transform: $F(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt$.
The table follows from the definition and parts: $1/s$, $1/(s - a)$, $n!/s^{n+1}$, the sine and cosine rows, and the shift rule.
$\mathcal{L}\{f'\} = sF - f(0)$ turns derivatives into algebra, starting values included.

formula.name: Laplace transform
formula.note: A present value at the continuous rate $s$.

summary.trap: Using $1/(s - a)$ at $s \le a$: there the integral diverges, so a negative price means nothing.

byKey.plus: You used $1/(s + a)$. The growth is subtracted from the rate.

options.why: You dropped the starting values. Each use of the derivative rule leaves one.
The rule is applied twice, so $f(0)$ picks up a factor of $s$.
You swapped the starting values. The $s$ multiplies $f(0)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply $\mathcal{L}\{g'\} = sG - g(0)$ with $g = f'$.

explain.text: $\mathcal{L}\{f''\} = s\mathcal{L}\{f'\} - f'(0) = s(sF - f(0)) - f'(0)$. That is $s^2F - sf(0) - f'(0)$.

byKey.cos: That is $s/(s^2 + b^2)$, the cosine's transform.

options.why: Positive rates are not enough: at $s = 1$ the integrand is $e^{t}$.
You added the growth to the rate. The exponent is $-(s - 2)t$.
At $s \le 2$ the integrand never decays, so the integral diverges.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Combine the exponents.

explain.text: The integrand is $e^{-(s - 2)t}$. It decays only when $s > 2$, and then the integral is $1/(s - 2)$.
